summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
Per GAO, twenty of 23 federal agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of the reported use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production; in about 200 instances, agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases. Agency reported uses included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. Some agencies are also using AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets.

The federal money and coordination picture is partial. GAO notes that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence, both fully implementing selected requirements. But OMB has not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and OPM has not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. State legislation names settings such as companion chatbots, political ads, insurance prior authorization, classrooms, and state agencies, indicating where lawmakers see AI in use.

The sources do not report measured return on investment for government AI. GAO's finding that most use cases are still in planning and only about 200 are currently used suggests production evidence is limited. No source in this set gives cost savings, efficiency gains, or outcome improvements from deployed government AI.

On risk and regulatory posture, Stanford HAI says this year's Index reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology falling behind and data transparency declining. OECD.AI gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, and in July 2024 the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership. The AI laws tracker on this site counts 5,959 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan. Of enrolled measures compared, 101 measures across 27 states were reviewed on September 18, 2026, and no two states wrote the same law. Only Colorado and Texas passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors; every other measure names one setting.

Per the AI laws tracker, no state created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act. A private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. The recurring duties are to tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits, or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of the user for conversational products, and keep records of what the system does because the attorney general is the enforcer most likely to meet. GAO adds that without government-wide guidance on acquiring and using AI, agencies cannot consistently manage AI, and until all requirements are met, agencies cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits. A reader deciding whether to deploy in government should expect a patchwork of state rules, human review requirements, recordkeeping duties, and enforcement by attorneys general rather than a single federal regulator.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports tracking 5,953 artificial intelligence bills across 53 US jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database. It also reviews 101 enacted measures across 27 states as of September 18, 2026, finding that no two states wrote the same law. Common patterns include requiring human involvement in decisions about health, employment, benefits, or education, and enforcement often falls to state attorneys general rather than new agencies. The page states that building to these recurring duties covers the obligations that appear most often.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
